assessment.nobel_worthiness: The observation of a Higgs-like boson at 125 GeV by two independent experiments closed the Standard Model's central open question and is exactly the kind of clue from nature that vindicates theory. The 2013 prize recognised the theoretical mechanism; the experimental discovery has no prize of its own and the committee would expect to complete the story.
assessment.attribution: The experimental credit is shared by thousands, so any trio is a compromise. Della Negra and Jenni conceived and led the ATLAS and CMS projects; Gianotti led ATLAS at the time of the announcement. Virdee is the equally strong CMS counterpart, so a two-ATLAS, one-CMS balance is debatable and I would want the experts' views on it.
assessment.maturity: Mature: independently confirmed by two experiments, with coupling measurements through Run 2 and Run 3 consistent with the Standard Model. Recognition is, if anything, overdue.
uncertainties: Whether the prize should honour the discovery, the detector and project leadership, or the accelerator builders (the LHC itself is a separate candidate).
Choice of three among several founders and spokespersons of ATLAS and CMS is inherently contested.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: IceCube opened neutrino astronomy by detecting a diffuse high-energy astrophysical neutrino flux, then associating neutrinos with the blazar TXS 0506+056 and the Galactic plane. A new window on the universe, with an observational clarity I value.
assessment.attribution: Halzen was the driving force behind IceCube and the instrument concept; Spiering is a long-standing leader of the field and the AMANDA-IceCube era. Credit for the original idea of deep-ice detection (and for earlier pioneering efforts such as DUMAND and Baikal) is a possible complication, but the supplied pair is defensible.
assessment.maturity: Reasonably mature: the diffuse flux is well established with multiple analyses, and source identification is progressing, though only a few sources are firmly associated.
uncertainties: Source associations remain few and statistically modest.
Priority questions relative to earlier detector pioneers and the large collaboration.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: GW170817 and its kilonova showed that neutron-star mergers make heavy r-process elements such as gold, linking gravitational waves, nuclear physics and the origin of the elements, with a clear existential dimension. The theory preceded the observation, and the observation confirmed it.
assessment.attribution: Lattimer (early r-process ejecta from mergers) and Metzger (kilonova modelling) are plausible theory pillars, and Tanvir represents the observational discovery of the kilonova. Other key people (for example Li and Paczynski for the kilonova concept, and the many GW170817 observers) are not in the supplied list, so the attribution is incomplete and could be unfair.
assessment.maturity: Fairly mature after GW170817 and later kilonova candidates, but it rests largely on one multi-messenger event; the fraction of r-process material from mergers versus other sites is still debated.
uncertainties: Dependence on a single golden event.
Attribution among theorists and observers is unresolved and partly outside the credited names.
Partial overlap with the 2017 LIGO prize.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Horizon-scale images of M87* and Sgr A* are direct empirical evidence on the nature of black holes and a visually striking, widely understood result. As someone working on horizonless alternatives I find it especially interesting that these images constrain such mimickers only partially.
assessment.attribution: Falcke proposed the shadow imaging approach, Doeleman led the EHT VLBI effort and Moran contributed the mm-VLBI foundations. A reasonable trio, though the EHT collaboration is large and the key technical contributors are many.
assessment.maturity: Moderately mature: two independent sources imaged and polarisation results published, but interpretation of ring size, spin and accretion models is still evolving, and black holes were recognised in 2017 and 2020.
uncertainties: Model-dependent interpretation of the images.
Recent recognition of black-hole physics may reduce urgency.
Large collaboration makes a three-person limit awkward.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Theoretical identification of the magic angle and the experimental discovery of correlated insulators and superconductivity in twisted bilayer graphene created the field of moire quantum matter. Importance and originality are high, and it is a case where theory and experiment met.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald made the flat-band prediction; Jarillo-Herrero's group delivered the experimental discovery. The credit is clean in structure, though other experimental groups and later theorists have contributed.
assessment.maturity: Maturing quickly: many groups reproduce the phases, but the nature of the superconductivity and correlated states is still debated, so it may be somewhat early.
uncertainties: Pairing mechanism and interpretation of the phases are unsettled.
Reproducibility depends on sample quality and twist-angle disorder.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Inflation and the quantum origin of structure explain the flatness, homogeneity and primordial perturbations of the universe, and the predicted spectrum is borne out by CMB data. The idea is of profound importance for our understanding of the universe.
assessment.attribution: Guth, Linde and Mukhanov are a plausible trio (the idea, the new and chaotic inflation scenarios, and the quantum fluctuation calculation), though Starobinsky, Albrecht and Steinhardt and others complicate the story. The credited names include duplicate spellings; I use one.
assessment.maturity: Mixed: the scalar spectrum is confirmed, but the inflaton and primordial gravitational waves have not been observed, so a decisive test is still lacking. Given my own work on trans-Planckian signatures I am wary of treating the theory as proven.
uncertainties: No detection of primordial B-modes; many inflation models fit.
Contested priority among several originators.
Persistent debate about whether inflation is predictive.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks at the 10^-18 level are the most precise measurement devices ever built and open tests of fundamental constants, relativity and perhaps dark-matter searches, tying precision metrology to fundamental physics.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice clock; Ye's group brought it to extreme precision. This credit is relatively clean, with others (for example single-ion clock pioneers) already recognised or arguably separate.
assessment.maturity: Mature on the technical side with multiple independent clocks, though a redefinition of the second is pending, and the fundamental-physics payoff is still prospective.
uncertainties: Impact on fundamental physics beyond metrology is not yet realised.
Overlap with earlier prizes for optical frequency combs and ion-trap work.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices realise the Hubbard model and other many-body Hamiltonians under controllable conditions, with the Mott transition as a landmark. The field links atomic physics, condensed matter and quantum information.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller proposed the Hubbard-model realisation (with Jaksch) and the quantum simulation program, while Bloch, Greiner and Esslinger carried out the decisive experiments. Choosing three from five leaves much unresolved, and Greiner and Esslinger are arguably as important as Bloch.
assessment.maturity: Mature in terms of experimental capability, but the scientific payoff in solving open many-body questions is still developing, and it overlaps with prior atomic-physics prizes.
uncertainties: Unclear whether quantum simulation has yet answered an open condensed-matter question.
Allocation among five credited names is difficult.
Overlap with B061, a separate candidate on the same theory.
